title: The Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants 2
full_review:
"The Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants 2" (Warner Bros.) finds friends Tibby (Amber Tamblyn), Lena (Alexis Bledel), Carmen (America Ferrera) and Bridget (Blake Lively) -- last seen as high school sophomores -- reuniting, albeit briefly, after their first year of college.

Once they scatter again for their disparate summer adventures, the symbol of their bond -- the titular, quasi-mystical pair of blue jeans they take turns wearing -- resumes its rounds via mail and FedEx. New York University film student Tibby, for one, wears them as she struggles to complete a screenplay while working in a Greenwich Village video store and pursuing romance with boyfriend Brian (Leonardo Lam).

 

Aspiring stage technician Carmen, who originally planned to stay home, can't face the tumult resulting from her mother's (Rachel Ticotin) pregnancy and her family's move to a new house. So, at the suggestion of actress friend Julia (Rachel Nichols), she escapes to a Vermont theater camp where she meets British actor Ian (Tom Wisdom), who thinks she, too, belongs on stage.

Bridget takes off to Turkey for an archaeological dig supervised by wisely maternal Professor Nasrin Mehani (Shohreh Aghdashloo), and reconnects with her estranged grandmother, Greta (Blythe Danner). Separated from her first love, Kostos (Michael Rady), Rhode Island art student Lena begins to fall for fellow dauber (and model) Leo (Jesse Williams).

 

The romantic comedy is briskly directed by Sanaa Hamri from Ann Brashares' novels. Uniformly competent performances are rather outshone by the New England and Greek isle settings.

One of the main story lines in this overcrowded but mostly enjoyable romantic comedy concerns an unplanned pregnancy. Though treated with due gravity -- with the young man prepared to make sacrifices to provide support -- the underlying moral issues are skimmed over.

 

Toward the end, there's an implied nonmarital encounter.

The self-confidence and creative endeavors of the main characters -- achievers all -- make them positive, if perhaps slightly unrealistic, role models.

The film contains implied nonmarital sexual activity, condom use, a suicide theme, a couple of profanities, and one crude and a few crass words; it is acceptable for older adolescents. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
